Honeymoon from Hell

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
Well known Adventurer Riaan Manser - raconteur with great footage
dragging his wife on a terrifying journey across the Pacific ocean and surviving. What more do you need to keep bums on seats

Summary:
For three months adventurer Riaan Manser took his new wife on a honeymoon they will never forget. Rowing from California to Hawaai. The Mansers recently returned to dry land and are enjoying every moment at their home in Betty’s Bay. Carte Blanche brings you the Honeymoon from Hell.



Further information:
The smash was a brutal one. Blood pouring down my face and neck. The warmth almost comforting but that smell too eerie. The wave had hit us from our starboard side; we had dropped in between two 4 metre swell side on, and were in for a huge wake up call. It is 4.30 am in the freezing cold North East Pacific, we were seconds before fast asleep inside our tiny Ocean Rowing boat cabin. Vasti and I lay shoulder to shoulder with our damp sleeping bags draped over our shivering bodies. I always sleep on the side of the wave's impact, and am immediately lifted and catapulted to the opposite cabin wall. My head making first contact with the fire extinguisher, then my body almost weightless now comes down onto a stunned Vasti. We both don't know what has happened. We just know that it is bad. Water is gushing into the cabin through the hatch and we are both standing on the roof of our boat cabin. We are upside down. I look out the glass hatch door to a scene similar to what the Two Oceans Aquarium offers their visitors. We are underwater with the mast light providing clarity on the boat exterior. A million thoughts run through my mind. “Did Vasti get hurt when I fell on her? What was that cracking sound as I hit the wall? Will we drown?
“Get up and help me flip the boat to its natural position! Quick quick" Was the first I shouted to Vasti. She was still stunned and quiet. We pushed the boat back with two heaves. The noise of all the cabin goods falling to where it should be almost a comforting sound. The splash of water at our feet certainly wasn't. I shout for Vasti to try save anything she can in the cabin and put any heavy object away. I get up and get outside to do two things. One to turn our rudder so we are not going broadside to the swell and two, assess outside damage and losses. I smell it again. That intense rich smell of fresh blood was deep in my lungs and the bitterness I tasted in my mouth. I was leaning over the smaller back hatch adjusting the rudder while the blood poured from my head. "I’ll be ok” I thought, "If it’s really bad I wouldn’t be able to be out here in this storm would I?"
I returned to the cabin with Vasti frantically saving all she could. Towels and sleeping bags absorbing most of the water. She was shocked and in tears. I sat down, sealed our hatch again and looked at her. I felt guilty. I dint want her in any danger. Especially not this kind of danger. Vasti began crying even more now, reaching out to my head and asking me if I was ok. "You are full of blood, we must stop the bleeding, how are you feeling, come here." This was the second night of On Honeymoon and a wakeup call for us both.

Vasti and I both talk a lot about how this fear never leaves you. It sits in your gut, eating away at any chance of you relaxing. We have probably only had 1 good night’s rest in the first 15 days, all thanks to these brewing nerves we are unable to control. Hold thumbs for us. We have had some technical issues which would probably have seen many a row boat pack their ocean crossing attempt in. Day 1 we had our auto pilot system give us problems. The auto pilot is the navigational equipment that continually adjusts your rudder so that the boat points in the correct direction. We just have to row fast enough for it to operate. Our rudder system though has many sticky points in its movement and sometimes stops moving entirely. All it really means is that we will row a bit more than the 4000KM originally planned.
Our second technicality involves our sea to sea communication. The VHF radio is a top of the range system that allows you to speak to any ship traffic within a few miles of us. Vital considering none of them can actually see us! We will need to do the obvious checks first, loose wires, proper connections etc, before panicking. Fortunately Seaport Supplies insisted we take a spare portable Raymarine VHF radio. We have used this radio successfully with three tankers to date to communicate our position in their path. It never astounds me how calm and relaxed these captains are with us taking on the ocean in a 6 meter rowing boat. At night watching the footage shot with our Gear 360 camera capture the sheer size of these tankers in the distance and Vasti says they definitely don't know what we really are. Probably thinking we are a small sailboat with an engine to boot.

Press Release:


Honeymoon Castaways
What constitutes a dream honeymoon? How does a terrifying row across the Pacific with the love of your life sound? Riaan Manser and his new wife Vasti decided they wanted a story to tell their children, so the couple embarked on a trip to Hawaii in a one ton rowing craft. Two days in, they were hit by a huge wave in the dark and their craft capsized. Carte Blanche joins the Mansers for a frank and amusing reflection on the most dangerous trip explorer Riaan has ever undertaken.


Script:


HONEYMOON FROM HELL FINAL SCRIPT TX 30th October 2016

Commentary one
Vasti Geldenhuys has spent a lot of time waiting for Riaan Manser to return home

First he rode around Africa on a bicycle, then he circumnavigated Madagascar alone on a kayak and in 2011, accompanied by Dan Skinstad, he went around Iceland

Up Sound Iceland

Commentary Two
Vasti, an advocate in Cape Town has been patient for 17 long years.

But in 2014 she said let’s go to New York. Fine, said Manser we will row there.
11 000 kilometres later, they made a decision they would never do anything like that again
Finally, this year they married.

Riaan
Shame we did say we would never row again and then we climbed into the boat.

Commentary Three
Their honeymoon began in Monterey Bay, close to San Fransisco. Destination Hawaii.
It was July, and they were heading straight into a record number of hurricanes and tropical storms

John Link
They wanted to have a story to tell their children …they had no idea how much their minds, bodies and relationship would be tested

Waves on boat up sound

Riaan
That is a brave place to go and row, a brave place, you are actually taking on an ocean that is saying we don’t want you here

Vasti Manser
The carbon fibre of our boat is this thick and its only that thickness that separates you from that ocean and what is going on outside

Up sound Yoh! Yoh! Yoh!

Commentary Four
At 4am on the second day their small craft was caught between two different weather systems colliding



Riaan
So its these long, long swells and at the top they are breaking and if you are in the top our one ton little boat is a matchstick picked up and thrown or we believe we were smashed by a wave from the side

Commentary five
Riaan slept starboard side where the waves were breaking

Riaan
The first thing I remember it was a loud, loud noise like a car accident

Vasti
I woke up with Riaan on top of me screaming we have to turn the boat around, we have to turn the boat around

Commentary six
Riaan had smashed his head against the fire extinguisher, but that was the least of his worries

Riaan
What really shocked me was to see the hatch that normally lets you see the sky – the mast light lighting up the freezing cold ocean below us– a lot of emotions and a lot of fear

John
In that moment the obvious conclusion is we could drown?
Vasti
I didn’t even think about drowning I think you just think about what you need to do to get out of the situation

Commentary seven
The boat is designed to right itself so they had to move quickly before the gushing water made it too heavy

Riaan
And I just had Vasti and me like mice in a hamster wheel trying to turn the boat back up

Up sound water exterior on boat

Commentary eight
Hours later Vasti was still in a bad way

Vasti Crying
Hey liefling what’s wrong
Your head
Hey its not that bad


John
You were weeping at one stage?
Vasti
I was weeping not only on that day John I was weeping a lot probably for the first three weeks
Vasti
How am I going to remove your hair
Riaan
Just move it and if we have to shave ok

Vasti Cries

Riaan
Vasti was very emotional after we capsized and I didn’t know how it had affected her until she told me what she had written in her diary – what would I do if I only had three days to live

Commentary nine
With no support and 2200 kilometres from land anything could happen

Up sound Vasti
I just called my dad to tell him we are ok and I am trying to decide if its worth it and I don’t think so

Vasti
I wrote in my diary / every day is miserable and then the next day its miserable – I always
started my diary with its miserable its miserable and that was our honeymoon

Commentary ten
For the first three weeks they hardly saw the sun, but they did see a lot of plastic
Vasti
We have a line of site about ten metres from each side of the boat and when we were rowing we would see some kind of plastic floating by

Commentary eleven
Their 12 hour days were spent mostly rowing with a break for lunch. They dragged lines hoping to catch dinner with a movie

Vasti
And then we would watch a movie on the computer. We always fall asleep
Rian
we have seen the beginning of a lot of movies

Commentary twelve
But during the day their bodies were pounded by the hours of rowing


Vasti
Your body just deteriorates, I think my knees were the worst

Riaan
Rowing allows you to have a passive movement because it’s a pull back and lats core of power but surprisingly your knees take a lot of strain

John
And some of the ailments have their own names –there is something that happens to your backside?
Riaan
We went through a lot of Vaseline
John
Laughs.. ..just through the daytime

Backside, oof! it makes life comfortable!

Riaan
Just too when you have this portion of your behind and doing this a few thousand times a day you need Vaseline to assist you

LINK
After making it through hurricane alley and violent storms on the 5th August they reached the halfway point. Suddenly the sun came out and everything seemed a little easier

Up Sound Yay

Commentary thirteen
Vasti had stopped counting the days and the sun improved her mood

John
when you finally made it to Hawaii what was the overriding emotions
Vasti
I think it was relief
Riaan
A week after we landed two hurricanes crossed our path where we would have been

Commentary fourteen
They had completed the journey in 39 days and broken the world record for the fastest row
across the Pacific from America to Hawaii

Vasti
Well we did row a lot so it wasn’t an accident but it wasn’t our goal and we ended up breaking the overall record which was set by a four man team just a month before us
Riaan
I don’t think those four men are going to tell people that their record was broken by two people on honeymoon
John
That is true and they have also probably stopped rowing

Commentary fifteen
Somewhere in their quest for survival, romance took a back seat

John
Was there a sense of it being a honeymoon was there
Riaan
It’s a gentleman you don’t speak out
John
I am trying to skirt around the issues here
Riaan
I think Posh spice called her one child Brooklyn- we aren’t going to be calling our child Pacific

THE END
Duration 08 min 03 seconds


In at 00: 01: 00:00
Out at

PROMO ONE 10 seconds 00: 09 30: 00
Riaan Manser and his wife Vasti went on honey moon and broke a world record for the fastest row across the Pacific to Hawaii without even trying.

PROMO TWO 15 seconds 00:10:00:00
Imagine being upside down in a tiny boat in the dark on a stormy Pacific Ocean

Riaan
What really shocked me– the mast light lighting up the freezing cold ocean below us– a lot of emotions and a lot of fear

PROMO THREE 15 seconds 00:10:30:00
They spent their honeymoon rowing across the Pacific encountering hurricanes and storms along the way
Vasti
I always started my diary with its miserable its miserable and that was our honeymoon








NOTES
They left from Monterray Bay on the 15th July in the morning. That is about an hour’s drive from San Fransisco – it took them 39 days and they arrived in Hawaii on the 23rd August at 09 05 am – unwittingly breaking the world record for rowing across the Pacific from North America to Hawaii

OUT TAKES

I was thinking about the storms hitting us every day and I was thinking if I could just row that would be fine /the guy that was giving us weather would say its turning into a storm or a tropical hurricane it was very stressful

I think we washed our hair once. Every single time we took a step outside we would clip ourselves in …*** sitting on the bucket doing your private business and being thrown across the deck was a challenge

Riaan
After I realized that we were really in a position where we could die- now you have taken Vasti life and put it slap bang in the middle of the most dangerous place you could ever be

metadata.Further information: The smash was a brutal one. Blood pouring down my face and neck. The warmth almost comforting but that smell too eerie. The wave had hit us from our starboard side; we had dropped in between two 4 metre swell side on, and were in for a huge wake up call. It is 4.30 am in the freezing cold North East Pacific, we were seconds before fast asleep inside our tiny Ocean Rowing boat cabin. Vasti and I lay shoulder to shoulder with our damp sleeping bags draped over our shivering bodies. I always sleep on the side of the wave's impact, and am immediately lifted and catapulted to the opposite cabin wall. My head making first contact with the fire extinguisher, then my body almost weightless now comes down onto a stunned Vasti. We both don't know what has happened. We just know that it is bad. Water is gushing into the cabin through the hatch and we are both standing on the roof of our boat cabin. We are upside down. I look out the glass hatch door to a scene similar to what the Two Oceans Aquarium offers their visitors. We are underwater with the mast light providing clarity on the boat exterior. A million thoughts run through my mind. “Did Vasti get hurt when I fell on her? What was that cracking sound as I hit the wall? Will we drown? “Get up and help me flip the boat to its natural position! Quick quick" Was the first I shouted to Vasti. She was still stunned and quiet. We pushed the boat back with two heaves. The noise of all the cabin goods falling to where it should be almost a comforting sound. The splash of water at our feet certainly wasn't. I shout for Vasti to try save anything she can in the cabin and put any heavy object away. I get up and get outside to do two things. One to turn our rudder so we are not going broadside to the swell and two, assess outside damage and losses. I smell it again. That intense rich smell of fresh blood was deep in my lungs and the bitterness I tasted in my mouth. I was leaning over the smaller back hatch adjusting the rudder while the blood poured from my head. "I’ll be ok” I thought, "If it’s really bad I wouldn’t be able to be out here in this storm would I?" I returned to the cabin with Vasti frantically saving all she could. Towels and sleeping bags absorbing most of the water. She was shocked and in tears. I sat down, sealed our hatch again and looked at her. I felt guilty. I dint want her in any danger. Especially not this kind of danger. Vasti began crying even more now, reaching out to my head and asking me if I was ok. "You are full of blood, we must stop the bleeding, how are you feeling, come here." This was the second night of On Honeymoon and a wakeup call for us both. Vasti and I both talk a lot about how this fear never leaves you. It sits in your gut, eating away at any chance of you relaxing. We have probably only had 1 good night’s rest in the first 15 days, all thanks to these brewing nerves we are unable to control. Hold thumbs for us. We have had some technical issues which would probably have seen many a row boat pack their ocean crossing attempt in. Day 1 we had our auto pilot system give us problems. The auto pilot is the navigational equipment that continually adjusts your rudder so that the boat points in the correct direction. We just have to row fast enough for it to operate. Our rudder system though has many sticky points in its movement and sometimes stops moving entirely. All it really means is that we will row a bit more than the 4000KM originally planned. Our second technicality involves our sea to sea communication. The VHF radio is a top of the range system that allows you to speak to any ship traffic within a few miles of us. Vital considering none of them can actually see us! We will need to do the obvious checks first, loose wires, proper connections etc, before panicking. Fortunately Seaport Supplies insisted we take a spare portable Raymarine VHF radio. We have used this radio successfully with three tankers to date to communicate our position in their path. It never astounds me how calm and relaxed these captains are with us taking on the ocean in a 6 meter rowing boat. At night watching the footage shot with our Gear 360 camera capture the sheer size of these tankers in the distance and Vasti says they definitely don't know what we really are. Probably thinking we are a small sailboat with an engine to boot.
